title: Beekeeping
materialsRequired: Sugar syrup (1:1 for spring, 2:1 for fall)
body:
## Overview

Bees pollinate ⅓ of crops and produce honey, wax, and propolis. A single
hive can yield 20–40 kg of honey per year.

## Prerequisites

- [Simple Tools](../survival/simple-tools.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Hive (Langstroth or top-bar)
- Smoker
- Hive tool
- Bee suit, gloves, veil
- Sugar syrup (1:1 for spring, 2:1 for fall)

## Procedure

### Catching a Swarm

1. Find a swarm on a branch in spring.
2. Shake into a box; cover quickly.
3. Transfer to a hive at dusk.

### Building a Colony

1. Install the swarm; leave alone 1 week.
2. Inspect weekly in spring/summer.
3. Feed sugar syrup until comb is drawn.

### Harvesting Honey

1. Wait until ⅔ of cells are capped.
2. Brush bees off frames; use a bee escape board.
3. Uncapp with a knife.
4. Extract with a centrifuge or crush-and-strain.
5. Leave 15 kg honey for the colony's winter.

### Winterizing

1. Reduce entrance.
2. Feed 2:1 syrup in fall.
3. Insulate; ensure ventilation to prevent condensation.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Bee stings can cause anaphylaxis. Have epinephrine if allergic.
- Smoke calms but does not sedate; work slowly.
- Africanized bees are aggressive — do not work them without experience.

title: Composting
materialsRequired: Greens: kitchen scraps, grass clippings, manure
body:
## Overview

Compost converts waste into fertility. It requires four ingredients:
carbon ("browns"), nitrogen ("greens"), water, and air.

## Prerequisites

- [Soil Testing](soil-testing.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Browns: dry leaves, straw, cardboard
- Greens: kitchen scraps, grass clippings, manure
- Pitchfork
- Water

## Procedure

### Pile Construction

1. Build a 1 m³ pile.
2. Layer 3 parts browns to 1 part greens.
3. Add water until the pile feels like a wrung-out sponge.
4. Turn every 3 days for hot compost (reaches 55–65°C).
5. Ready in 4–8 weeks when cool, earthy, and crumbly.

### Sheet Composting (No-Turn)

1. Spread browns and greens directly on the soil.
2. Cover with mulch.
3. Worms and microbes do the work over 6–12 months.

### Trench Composting

1. Dig a 30 cm trench.
2. Bury kitchen scraps.
3. Cover with soil.
4. Plant above after 1 month.

### Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| Smells rotten | Too wet, no air | Turn, add browns |
| Not heating up | Too dry, not enough greens | Water, add greens |
| Attracts pests | Meat/dairy in pile | Bury deep, omit these |

## Safety Notes

- Do not compost meat, dairy, or pet waste in open piles.
- Hot compost kills pathogens; cold compost does not.
- Wash hands after handling.

title: Crop Rotation
body:
## Overview

Rotation breaks pest cycles, balances nutrients, and prevents soil depletion.
Rule: never plant the same family in the same bed two years in a row.

## Prerequisites

- [Soil Testing](soil-testing.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Map of plots
- Seeds for 4 families

## Procedure

### The Four-Family Rotation

| Year | Bed 1 | Bed 2 | Bed 3 | Bed 4 |
|------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| 1 | Legume | Brassica | Root | Fruiting |
| 2 | Brassica | Root | Fruiting | Legume |
| 3 | Root | Fruiting | Legume | Brassica |
| 4 | Fruiting | Legume | Brassica | Root |

Families:
- **Legume:** pea, bean, clover — fixes nitrogen
- **Brassica:** cabbage, broccoli, kale — heavy feeder
- **Root:** carrot, beet, onion — loosens soil
- **Fruiting:** tomato, pepper, squash — heavy feeder

### Cover Crops

- Winter: rye, vetch, clover
- Summer: buckwheat, cowpea
- Chop and till in before seed set to add organic matter.

### Fallow

- Rest a bed every 4 years.
- Plant with a legume cover and let it mature.

## Safety Notes

- Do not rotate tomatoes with potatoes (same family, shared diseases).
- Do not follow a legume with another legume.

title: Food Preservation

sources.title: USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning

body:
## Overview

Preservation extends harvest into winter. Methods: drying, salting, smoking,
canning, fermenting, and root cellaring.

## Prerequisites

- [Making Fire](../survival/making-fire.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Drying rack
- Salt
- Glass jars with lids
- Smokehouse
- Root cellar

## Procedure

### Sun Drying

1. Slice food 3–6 mm thick.
2. Lay on a rack in full sun, covered with mesh.
3. Turn daily; dry 2–5 days until leathery.
4. Rehydrate in water before use.

### Salting

1. Layer food with coarse salt (1 kg salt per 4 kg food).
2. Weight down; keep submerged in brine.
3. Ready in 2–6 weeks.
4. Rinse before eating.

### Smoking

1. Build a small fire in a smokehouse.
2. Use hardwood (hickory, oak, apple). Never resinous softwoods.
3. Cold smoke (20–30°C) for 1–3 days for preservation.
4. Hot smoke (60–80°C) for immediate consumption.

### Water-Bath Canning (High-Acid Foods)

1. Sterilize jars in boiling water.
2. Fill with hot food, leaving 1 cm headspace.
3. Seal; process in boiling water for the recipe time.
4. Cool; check seal (lid should not flex).

### Pressure Canning (Low-Acid Foods)

1. Use a pressure canner at 10 PSI (115°C) for low-acid foods (meat, beans).
2. Water-bath canning does **not** kill botulism spores.

### Fermenting

1. Submerge vegetables in 2% brine.
2. Keep anaerobic; weight down.
3. Ferment 1–4 weeks at 18–22°C.
4. Refrigerate when sour to taste.

### Root Cellaring

1. Ideal: 0–4°C, 90–95% humidity, dark.
2. Store root vegetables in sand or straw.
3. Ventilate to prevent ethylene buildup.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Botulism from improperly canned low-acid foods is often fatal.
- Discard any can with bulging lid, off-smell, or cloudiness.
- Boil all home-canned low-acid food for 10 minutes before eating.

title: Grain Cultivation
body:
## Overview

Grains (wheat, rice, maize, barley, millet) provide the calorie base of
civilization. They store dry for years.

## Prerequisites

- [Soil Testing](soil-testing.md)
- [Crop Rotation](crop-rotation.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Seed grain
- Plow or hoe
- Sickle or scythe
- Threshing surface
- Winnowing basket
- Mill (see [Mills](../materials/mills.md))

## Procedure

### Soil Preparation

1. Test soil; amend with compost to pH 6–7.
2. Plow to 15–20 cm.
3. Harrow to break clods.

### Sowing

1. Broadcast or drill seed at the rate for your grain:
   - Wheat: 100–150 kg/ha
   - Rice (transplanted): 40–60 kg/ha
   - Maize: 20–25 kg/ha
2. Cover lightly with soil.

### Growing

1. Water: 400–650 mm per season for wheat; rice needs flooding.
2. Weed at 3 weeks and 6 weeks.
3. Watch for rust, blight, and locusts.

### Harvest

1. Cut when grain is hard and heads nod.
2. Bundle into shocks; dry in the field 1–2 weeks.
3. Thresh by beating bundles on a hard surface.
4. Winnow by tossing in the wind.

### Storage

1. Dry grain to <12% moisture (bites crack, not dent).
2. Store in airtight containers with desiccant.
3. Add diatomaceous earth to prevent weevils.
4. Cool, dark, dry place. Viability: 5–20 years.

## Safety Notes

- Ergot (fungal infection of rye) is toxic — discard black grains.
- Grain dust is explosive; ventilate threshing areas.
- Rice paddies breed mosquitoes; manage standing water.

title: Grain Storage and Pest Control
yield: A 1 m3 bin holds roughly 600-800 kg of dry grain
season: Immediately after harvest; cool, dry grain stores best
storage: Dry to 12-14% moisture; 6-24 months in hermetic or well-sealed storage
hazards: Mould and aflatoxin from damp grain
materialsRequired: Raised, sealed bin or hermetic bags
body:
## Overview

Grain that is stored wet or warm can lose a season's work to mould, insects,
and rodents in weeks. The two decisive variables are moisture and temperature:
dry grain below about 12-14% moisture, kept cool and sealed, stores for 6-24
months. A 1 m³ bin holds roughly 600-800 kg of grain.

## Prerequisites

- Grain cultivation and harvesting
- A dry, raised storage site

## Materials & Tools

- Raised, sealed bin or hermetic storage bags
- Moisture meter
- Clean tarps and pallets
- Diatomaceous earth
- Rodent-proof mesh
- Labels and a record book

## Procedure

### 1. Harvest and dry

1. Harvest at maturity and avoid mixing wet or mouldy grain with good grain.
2. Dry to 12-14% moisture; test with a moisture meter, not by bite.
3. Dry on clean tarps, in thin layers, with airflow and sun.
4. Cool the grain before storage; warm grain sweats as it cools.

### 2. Clean and prepare the store

1. Winnow or sieve out chaff, broken kernels, and dust.
2. Clean the bin, remove old grain, and repair holes and gaps.
3. Raise the bin off the floor and keep it away from walls.
4. Fit rodent mesh over vents and keep the lid sealed.

### 3. Fill and protect

1. Fill the bin in one session and level the surface.
2. Use hermetic bags for small quantities; seal them fully.
3. Mix diatomaceous earth at the label rate for insect control where approved.
4. Label each lot with the harvest date and moisture reading.

### 4. Monitor and treat

1. Check monthly for warmth, condensation, insects, or rodent droppings.
2. Probe the centre and bottom; a hot spot means mould or insects.
3. Remove and use affected grain first; do not mix it with clean grain.
4. Fumigate only with trained help and approved products; never in a living
   space.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Mouldy grain can contain aflatoxins that cause liver
  damage and cancer. Do not eat or feed visibly mouldy grain.
- Grain dust can explode. Ventilate, avoid open flames, and wear a mask when
  cleaning.
- Fumigants are highly toxic. Use only with training, respirators, and warning
  signs.
- Never enter a grain bin that may have bridged; engulfment can kill in
  seconds.

title: Raising Livestock
body:
## Overview

Livestock convert grass and waste into protein, fat, leather, and fertilizer.
Start small — chickens and rabbits first, then goats or pigs, then cattle.

## Prerequisites

- [Composting](composting.md)
- [Emergency Shelter](../survival/emergency-shelter.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Fencing
- Feed (grain, hay, forage)
- Water source
- Shelter
- Veterinary basics (see [Health](../health/README.md))

## Procedure

### Chickens

1. Coop: 0.4 m² per bird, roosts 30 cm off ground.
2. Feed: 100 g layer pellets per bird per day + forage.
3. Water: 250 mL per bird per day.
4. Eggs: 1 per hen per day in peak season.
5. Slaughter at 18–24 months for stewing hens.

### Rabbits

1. Hutch: 0.5 m² per adult.
2. Feed: hay ad libitum, 100 g pellets, greens.
3. Breeding: 1 buck per 10 does; gestation 30 days.
4. Yield: 4–8 kg meat per year per doe.

### Goats (Dairy)

1. Shelter: 2 m² per goat, dry bedding.
2. Feed: browse + 1 kg hay + 0.5 kg grain per day.
3. Milk: 2–4 L per day, twice daily.
4. Breeding: seasonal; gestation 150 days.

### Pigs

1. Pen: 10 m² per pig.
2. Feed: kitchen waste, grain, forage.
3. Farrowing: 1 litter per year, 8–12 piglets.
4. Slaughter at 6–8 months (100 kg).

### Cattle

1. Pasture: 0.4–1 ha per cow.
2. Feed: grass/hay + minerals.
3. Milk: 15–30 L/day for dairy breeds.
4. Breeding: 1 bull per 30 cows; gestation 280 days.

### Health Basics

- Quarantine new animals 2 weeks.
- Vaccinate per local disease profile.
- Deworm quarterly.
- Isolate sick animals immediately.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Zoonotic diseases (brucellosis, rabies, salmonella) transmit from animals.
- Always wash hands after handling.
- Bulls and boars can be aggressive; never turn your back.
- Slaughter humanely; stun before bleeding.

title: Seed Saving
body:
## Overview

Saved seed preserves genetic diversity and independence. Open-pollinated
(heirloom) varieties breed true; hybrids do not.

## Prerequisites

- [Soil Testing](soil-testing.md)
- [Crop Rotation](crop-rotation.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Healthy plants (select best specimens)
- Cloth bags
- Glass jars
- Silica desiccant

## Procedure

### Self-Pollinating (Tomato, Bean, Pea, Lettuce)

1. Let fruits mature fully on the plant.
2. For tomatoes: ferment seeds in water 3 days to remove gel.
3. Rinse, dry on a plate (not paper towel).
4. Store in a cool, dark, dry place.

### Cross-Pollinating (Corn, Squash, Brassicas)

1. Isolate varieties by 400 m or use hand-pollination.
2. Bag unopened flowers; hand-pollinate with a brush.
3. Re-bag until fruit sets.

### Biennials (Carrot, Onion, Cabbage)

1. Overwinter roots/bulbs.
2. Replant in spring.
3. Harvest seed heads when dry.

### Storage

1. Dry seeds to <10% moisture (they snap, not bend).
2. Store in glass jars with desiccant.
3. Label: species, variety, year, source.
4. Cool (5–10°C), dark, dry. Viability: 3–10 years.

## Safety Notes

- Do not save seed from diseased plants.
- Do not save seed from F1 hybrids.
- Label meticulously — misidentified seed is worse than no seed.

title: Soil Testing
body:
## Overview

Soil health determines crop yield. Test pH, texture, and organic matter
before planting.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Jar with lid
- Vinegar
- Baking soda
- Distilled water
- Shovel

## Procedure

### Jar Test (Texture)

1. Fill a jar ⅓ with soil, top with water, add a pinch of detergent.
2. Shake vigorously for 3 minutes.
3. Let settle 24 hours.
4. Measure layers: sand (bottom), silt, clay (top). Ratios indicate loam, sandy, or clay.

### pH Test (Vinegar & Baking Soda)

1. Place 2 tbsp soil in a cup.
2. Add vinegar. If it fizzes → alkaline (pH > 7).
3. If no fizz, repeat with baking soda + water. Fizz → acidic (pH < 7).
4. No reaction either way → neutral (pH ~7).

### Organic Matter Test

1. Weigh a dry soil sample.
2. Burn it in a fire-safe container until only ash remains.
3. Weight loss = organic matter content. Aim for 5%.

### Drainage Test

1. Dig a 30 cm hole; fill with water.
2. Refill after it drains. Measure time to drain second fill.
3. 2–4 cm/hour is ideal.

## Safety Notes

- Vinegar/baking soda reactions are harmless but messy.
- Burning soil releases smoke; do outdoors.

title: Bridges

sources.title: US Army FM 5-430 Roads and Airfields

body:
## Overview

Bridges cross water or ravines. Span length dictates the type: simple beam for short spans, trusses for medium, and suspension for long spans.

## Prerequisites

- Timber Framing
- Rope & Cordage

## Materials & Tools

- Heavy timbers or steel
- Stone abutments
- Rope or cable
- Fasteners and pegs

## Procedure

### Surveying the Crossing

1. Measure span, bank height, and flood level.
2. Choose an abutment site on firm ground above flood stage.

### Beam Bridge

1. Build abutments of stone or concrete.
2. Lay one or more beams across, sized by span and load.
3. Deck with planks and add railings.

### Truss or Suspension

1. Assemble a truss on the bank and roll it into place.
2. For suspension, anchor cables to deadmen and hang the deck.
3. Load-test gradually before allowing traffic.

## Safety Notes

- Red hazard: structural failure is often fatal; over-build and load-test.
- Never work over moving water without fall protection and a spotter.

title: Latrines & Sanitation

sources.title: WHO Guidelines on Sanitation and Health

body:
## Overview

Safe excreta disposal prevents cholera, typhoid, and intestinal worms. A fly-proof latrine and a handwashing point are the highest-impact sanitation interventions in any settlement.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Shovel
- Slab or timber cover
- Vent pipe and screen
- Water and soap or ash

## Procedure

### Pit Latrine

1. Dig a pit at least 1 m deep, away from wells (>=30 m) and downhill.
2. Fit a squat slab with a tight drop hole.
3. Build a shelter for privacy and a roof to keep rain out.

### Ventilated Improved Pit

1. Run a vent pipe from the pit to above the roof.
2. Screen the pipe top to trap flies.

### Handwashing Station

1. Set a tippy-tap or bucket with a spout near the exit.
2. Provide soap or wood ash before eating and after defecation.

## Safety Notes

- Never site pits uphill or within 30 m of a water source.
- Wash hands with soap; ash is an acceptable substitute.

title: Masonry
body:
## Overview

Masonry builds durable walls, foundations, and ovens from stone or brick bedded in lime or cement mortar. Correct bond and footing prevent collapse.

## Prerequisites

- Lime & Cement
- Brick Making

## Materials & Tools

- Stone or fired brick
- Lime or cement mortar
- Level, trowel, and string line

## Procedure

### Footing

1. Dig a trench below frost depth and fill with rubble set in mortar.
2. Level the first course carefully; every error propagates upward.

### Laying Units

1. Spread a mortar bed and place each unit, tapping it level.
2. Stagger joints (running bond) and keep the wall plumb with a string line.
3. Rake joints when mortar is thumb-dry, then point them.

### Curing

1. Keep masonry damp for several days to prevent cracking.
2. Cover in freezing weather until mortar hardens.

## Safety Notes

- Lime and cement are caustic; wear gloves and eye protection.
- Never build tall unsupported walls; brace until cured.

title: Roads & Drainage

sources.title: US Army FM 5-430 Roads and Airfields

body:
## Overview

All-weather roads move goods and people and connect settlements. The key is a crowned surface with side ditches so water leaves the roadbed quickly.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Gravel or crushed stone
- Hand tools and barrows
- Logs or culverts

## Procedure

### Alignment & Clearing

1. Lay out a route along ridges or valley sides, crossing streams at right angles.
2. Clear vegetation and topsoil from a 4-6 m corridor.

### Construction

1. Cut side ditches and crown the roadbed to shed water.
2. Spread and compact gravel in layers, largest stones at the base.
3. Install culverts at every drainage crossing.

## Safety Notes

- Brace trench sides during excavation.
- Keep ditches clear; a blocked ditch destroys a road in one storm.

title: Root Cellar Construction
yield: A 2 m x 3 m cellar holds roughly 1,500-2,500 kg of root crops and preserves
season: Build in dry weather; load after harvest and ventilate in cool nights
storage: Hold 0-4 C and 85-95% humidity; most root crops keep 3-8 months

sources.title: USDA Storage of Vegetables and Root Crops

body:
## Overview

A root cellar uses earth's stable temperature and high humidity to keep root
crops, apples, cabbages, and preserves through winter. A 2 m x 3 m cellar holds
roughly 1,500-2,500 kg. The design must balance insulation, ventilation, and
moisture: too warm and crops sprout or rot, too dry and they shrivel, too wet
and mould wins.

## Prerequisites

- Simple housing and earthwork experience
- A well-drained site

## Materials & Tools

- Stone or concrete block
- Timber or concrete roof
- Insulation
- Vent pipes with insect screen
- Gravel floor
- Shelving and slatted crates
- Thermometer and hygrometer
- Rodent mesh

## Procedure

### 1. Site and design

1. Choose a slope or high spot with good drainage; never a hollow that floods.
2. Keep the cellar away from septic fields, wells, and tree roots.
3. Plan two vents: a low inlet and a high outlet for natural convection.
4. Size for the harvest: about 0.5-0.7 tonnes per cubic metre of usable space.

### 2. Excavate and line

1. Mark the footprint and excavate with stable, sloped sides.
2. Shore the walls before digging deeper than 1 m.
3. Build block or stone walls with a footing; leave weep holes and a gravel
   drain.
4. Seal the outside against surface water and insulate the roof and upper
   walls.

### 3. Roof, door, and vents

1. Build a strong roof that can carry soil and snow load.
2. Fit an insulated, tight-fitting door; avoid a direct path for warm air.
3. Install screened vents with adjustable dampers.
4. Cover the roof with earth and vegetation, leaving the vents clear.

### 4. Load and manage

1. Cure root crops for a few days before storage; remove damaged produce.
2. Store in slatted crates off the floor, separated by crop and date.
3. Keep the temperature near 0-4 C and humidity at 85-95%.
4. Vent at night when outside air is colder; close vents in warm weather.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Excavations collapse. Shore walls and never let anyone work
  alone below ground.
- Carbon dioxide can accumulate in a sealed cellar. Open the door and ventilate
  before entering; use a lantern test or gas monitor.
- Mouldy produce releases spores; remove spoilage and wear a mask.
- Keep rodents out with mesh and concrete; they contaminate food and gnaw
  wiring.

title: Simple Housing
materialsRequired: Posts and beams (rot-resistant timber or treated poles)
Wattle, cordwood, adobe, or log infill
body:
## Overview

Permanent shelter protects against weather, pests, and temperature swings. A dry, ventilated, raised-floor structure with a sound roof and a hearth is enough for most climates.

## Prerequisites

- Emergency Shelter
- Rope & Cordage

## Materials & Tools

- Posts and beams (rot-resistant timber or treated poles)
- Wattle, cordwood, adobe, or log infill
- Roof thatch, shingles, or earth
- Stone or rubble for footings

## Procedure

### Site & Footings

1. Choose level, well-drained ground above flood lines.
2. Clear vegetation and mark a rectangle with corner stakes and string.
3. Set corner posts on dry-stacked stone footings to keep wood off the soil.

### Frame & Walls

1. Set vertical posts at 1.5-2 m spacing and brace them plumb.
2. Add a top plate and gable rafters.
3. Infill walls with wattle-and-daub, cordwood, or stacked logs.

### Roof & Floor

1. Lay purlins across the rafters and cover with thatch, shingles, or sod.
2. Overlap roofing layers so water always runs downhill.
3. Raise the floor 20-30 cm on joists and pack the crawl space with dry stone.

## Safety Notes

- Never burn unseasoned or resinous wood in a sealed room without ventilation.
- Treat all framing against insects and rot where possible.

title: Surveying
body:
## Overview

Surveying sets out boundaries, grades, and alignments accurately. Simple leveling and angle measurement suffice for most community works.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Level (water or dumpy)
- Measuring chain or tape
- Range poles and pegs
- Plumb bob

## Procedure

### Leveling

1. Use a water level (clear hose) or dumpy level to transfer elevations.
2. Record backsight, foresight, and rise/fall for each station.

### Setting Out

1. Establish a baseline and square it with the 3-4-5 method.
2. Offset to locate corners and alignments.
3. Mark stations with stakes and reference ties.

## Safety Notes

- Avoid stringing lines across roads or paths without flagging.

title: Timber Framing
materialsRequired: Chisels, augers, and a bow saw
body:
## Overview

Timber framing joins heavy members with interlocking mortise-and-tenon joints and pegs. A well-cut frame carries roof and floor loads without nails or steel.

## Prerequisites

- Simple Tools

## Materials & Tools

- Seasoned structural timber
- Hardwood pegs
- Chisels, augers, and a bow saw
- Mallet and framing square

## Procedure

### Layout

1. Square a frame on the ground using the 3-4-5 method.
2. Mark joints with a numbering system before cutting.

### Cutting Joints

1. Bore and chop mortises one-third the member's thickness.
2. Cut tenons to a snug fit; test each joint dry before assembly.

### Raising

1. Assemble bents flat, then raise them with props and pegs.
2. Join bents with girts and purlins, checking plumb and level.
3. Pin every joint with a draw-bored hardwood peg.

## Safety Notes

- Work with a spotter when raising bents; keep clear of falling members.
- Keep edged tools sheathed when not cutting.

title: Water Wells
body:
## Overview

A well taps groundwater for a reliable supply. The method depends on depth: dug wells for shallow aquifers, driven and bored wells for sand, and drilled wells for deep rock.

## Prerequisites

- Finding Water

## Materials & Tools

- Lining (stone, brick, or concrete rings)
- Pump or bucket hoist
- Rope and bucket

## Procedure

### Locating the Aquifer

1. Sight wells in low ground near streams, springs, or green vegetation.
2. Confirm with dowsing-free methods: test pits and local knowledge.

### Dug Well

1. Excavate a shaft 1 m wide, lining as you descend to prevent collapse.
2. Stop at the water table and line the intake with gravel.
3. Build a curb 50 cm above grade and cap to keep surface water out.

### Finishing

1. Backfill around the lining with clay to shed surface water.
2. Disinfect the well with chlorine and test before drinking.

## Safety Notes

- Dug wells can collapse or accumulate toxic gas; always have a spotter.
- Treat all well water as contaminated until disinfected.

title: Battery Basics
body:
## Overview

Batteries store electrical energy chemically. Lead-acid is the most
rebuildable chemistry; lithium-ion is denser but harder to make from scratch.

## Prerequisites

- [Metal Smelting](../materials/metal-smelting.md)
- [Chemistry](chemistry.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Lead plates (grid + active material)
- Sulfuric acid (30% H₂SO₄)
- Case (plastic or hard rubber)
- Separators (porous rubber, glass mat)
- Terminals

## Procedure

### Lead-Acid Cell (2 V per cell)

1. Cast lead grids; paste with lead oxide (positive) and sponge lead (negative).
2. Stack alternating plates with separators.
3. Weld straps to terminals.
4. Fill with 30% sulfuric acid.
5. **Formation charge:** slow charge for 24 hours to convert pastes.

### 6 Cells = 12 V Battery

- 6 cells in series → 12 V nominal.
- Capacity: Ah = plate area × number of plates.

### Charging

1. **Bulk:** constant current to 14.4 V.
2. **Absorption:** constant voltage 14.4 V until current drops to 3% of capacity.
3. **Float:** 13.6 V to maintain.

### Maintenance

- Top up with distilled water monthly.
- Equalize every 1–3 months (15.5 V for 2 hours).
- Never discharge below 50% (12.1 V).
- Keep terminals clean; grease them.

### Other Chemistries

- **NiFe (Edison):** 1.2 V/cell; nearly indestructible; low efficiency.
- **NiCd:** 1.2 V/cell; toxic cadmium.
- **LiFePO₄:** 3.2 V/cell; safe; requires BMS.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Sulfuric acid burns. Lead is neurotoxic.
  Wear gloves, goggles, apron. Work outdoors.
- **Explosive hydrogen** during charging — ventilate.
- Never short terminals; never reverse polarity.
- Dispose of lead and acid properly.

title: Biogas Digester
body:
## Overview

Anaerobic digestion of manure, food waste, and crop residue produces biogas
(60% CH₄, 40% CO₂) plus a nutrient-rich effluent for fertilizer.

## Prerequisites

- [Raising Livestock](../agriculture/raising-livestock.md)
- [Fire & Combustion](fire-combustion.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Digester (fixed-dome, floating-drum, or tubular)
- Feedstock: manure, food scraps
- Water
- Gas storage (bag or drum)
- Stove or generator

## Procedure

### Fixed-Dome (Deenbandhu)

1. Dig a pit 2–3 m diameter, 2 m deep.
2. Build brick or concrete dome over the top with a gas outlet.
3. Inlet pipe at bottom for slurry.
4. Outlet pipe for effluent at ⅔ height.
5. Volume: 1 m³ per cow per day.

### Floating-Drum

1. Dig a cylindrical pit.
2. Place a steel drum inverted over the top — it rises with gas pressure.
3. Gas outlet from drum top.

### Tubular (Flexible)

1. Lay a long plastic or rubber bag in a trench.
2. Fill ⅔ with slurry.
3. Gas collects at the top; use a weighted bag for pressure.

### Feeding

- Cow manure: 1:1 with water
- Pig manure: 1:2 with water
- Food waste: pre-compost, then feed
- C:N ratio: 20–30:1
- pH: 6.8–7.4
- Temperature: 30–40°C (mesophilic)

### Retention Time

- 15–30 days at 35°C.
- 40–60 days at 20°C.

### Using Biogas

- Burn directly in a stove (adjust air for methane).
- 1 m³ biogas ≈ 0.6 L petrol ≈ 6 kWh.
- 1 cow yields ~0.4 m³/day.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Biogas is explosive (5–15% in air) and can asphyxiate.
  Never enter a digester pit — H₂S and CO₂ displace oxygen.
- Keep flames away from gas leaks.
- Ventilate any enclosed gas equipment.
- Effluent is caustic; wear gloves.

title: Electrical Wiring
body:
## Overview

Wiring distributes electricity safely. Rules: correct wire gauge for current,
proper grounding, overcurrent protection, and secure connections.

## Prerequisites

- [Metal Smelting](../materials/metal-smelting.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Copper wire (various gauges)
- Insulation (rubber, cloth, plastic)
- Breakers or fuses
- Outlets, switches
- Conduit
- Multimeter

## Procedure

### Wire Gauge

| Current (A) | Copper Gauge (AWG) |
|-------------|-------------------|
| 10 | 16 |
| 15 | 14 |
| 20 | 12 |
| 30 | 10 |
| 50 | 6 |
| 100 | 2 |

Rule: voltage drop <3% over the run.

### Basic Circuit

1. Source → fuse/breaker → switch → load → return to source.
2. Ground the source (rod into earth).
3. Neutral and ground are separate at the panel; tied only at one point.

### Making Connections

1. Strip insulation 1 cm.
2. Twist wires (for solid) or crimp (for stranded).
3. Solder for permanent; wire nut for serviceable.
4. Wrap with electrical tape or heat-shrink.

### Installing a Breaker

1. Size to wire gauge (see table).
2. Connect hot wire to breaker; neutral to bus bar.
3. Ground wire to ground bar.
4. Test with a multimeter before energizing.

### Grounding

1. Copper rod 2.5 m into moist earth.
2. Bond to panel ground bar.
3. All metal enclosures must be grounded.

### Low-Voltage DC

- 12 V systems: fuse at 1.25× max current.
- Voltage drop over distance: use larger wire.
- Keep polarity consistent (red +, black −).

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Electrocution kills. De-energize before working.
- Test with a multimeter; never trust a switch.
- Lockout/tagout for shared systems.
- GFCI for wet locations.
- Do not overload circuits — fires start in walls.

title: Fire & Combustion
body:
## Overview

Combustion is the foundational energy conversion. Understanding the fire
triangle (fuel, oxygen, heat) enables efficient stoves, kilns, and furnaces.

## Prerequisites

- [Making Fire](../survival/making-fire.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Fuel (wood, charcoal, peat, dung)
- Firebox or stove
- Chimney or flue
- Air control

## Procedure

### The Fire Triangle

- Remove any leg → fire goes out.
- Control air → control heat.

### Wood Combustion Stages

1. **Drying** (<150°C): moisture evaporates.
2. **Pyrolysis** (150–300°C): volatiles release as smoke.
3. **Gas combustion** (300–600°C): flames consume volatiles.
4. **Char combustion** (600–1,000°C): glowing coals burn.

### Efficient Wood Stove

1. Firebox: 30 × 30 × 40 cm.
2. Air inlet at base with adjustable damper.
3. Baffle plate above fire to increase gas residence time.
4. Chimney: 4–6 m tall, insulated, with a cap.

### Rocket Stove (High Efficiency)

1. Build an L-shaped combustion chamber (J-tube).
2. Vertical riser: insulated, 3× cross-section of feed tube.
3. Heat exchanger at the top.
4. Fuel: small sticks, continuously fed.

### Charcoal Forge/Furnace

1. Charcoal burns at 1,200°C+ with forced air.
2. Use for blacksmithing, smelting, glass.
3. Bellows: bag, box, or centrifugal.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion kills.
  Always vent.
- Chimney fires: clean flues monthly.
- Never burn treated wood (arsenic, chromium).
- Keep a fire extinguisher or sand bucket nearby.

title: Micro-Hydro
body:
## Overview

Micro-hydro (up to 100 kW) provides continuous power where a stream drops
in elevation. It is more reliable than wind or solar.

## Prerequisites

- [Mills](../materials/mills.md)
- [Electrical Wiring](electrical-wiring.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Intake weir
- Penstock (pipe)
- Turbine (Pelton, Turgo, or crossflow)
- Generator
- Tailrace
- Wiring

## Procedure

### Site Assessment

1. Measure **head** (vertical drop) with a level and staff.
2. Measure **flow** with a weir or float method.
3. Power (W) ≈ head (m) × flow (L/s) × 5 (at 50% efficiency).

### Intake & Penstock

1. Build a small weir to divert part of the stream.
2. Settling basin to remove sediment.
3. Penstock: PVC, HDPE, or steel, sized for low friction.
4. Anchor every 3 m on slopes.

### Turbine Selection

- **Pelton:** high head (>20 m), low flow.
- **Turgo:** medium head (5–30 m), medium flow.
- **Crossflow:** low head (2–10 m), high flow.

### Generator

1. Direct-coupled PMG for battery charging.
2. Induction motor as generator for grid-tie.
3. Voltage regulation via electronic load controller.

### Electrical

1. Rectify AC → DC for battery charging.
2. Or use an induction generator and sync to grid.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Water under pressure cuts flesh. Never open a live penstock.
- Drowning risk in weirs and tailraces.
- Electrical hazards from wet environments; use GFCI.
- Fish passage may be required by law in some jurisdictions.

title: Solar Photovoltaic Systems
yield: About 3-5 kWh per day per 1 kW of panels in a sunny climate, after losses
season: Year-round; output drops in winter, haze, and shade
storage: Batteries should be ventilated, cool, and kept at 50-80% charge when not in use
hazards: Battery acid burns and hydrogen explosion
Fire from undersized wiring or fuses

sources.title: US Department of Energy Off-Grid PV Guidance

body:
## Overview

A solar photovoltaic system turns sunlight into electricity with no fuel and
few moving parts. A 1 kW array in a sunny climate produces roughly 3-5 kWh per
day after losses. The panels are only half the system: a charge controller,
battery bank, fuses, and correctly sized cable determine whether it is safe and
long-lived.

## Prerequisites

- Battery basics
- Electrical wiring skills

## Materials & Tools

- PV panels and mounting rails
- Charge controller sized for array current
- Battery bank, vented and secured
- Inverter if alternating current is needed
- Fuses, disconnects, and grounding hardware
- UV-rated cable and MC4 connectors

## Procedure

### 1. Audit the load

1. List every appliance and its watts times hours per day.
2. Add 20-30% for inverter and wiring losses.
3. Size the array for the worst month, not the best.
4. Size the battery for 1-3 days of autonomy, depending on critical loads.

### 2. Mount the array

1. Face the panels toward the equator: south in the northern hemisphere.
2. Tilt them at roughly the site latitude, steeper in winter if snow is common.
3. Keep panels clear of shade from trees, buildings, and each other.
4. Leave airflow behind the panels and secure rails for wind load.

### 3. Wire and protect

1. Connect panels in series or parallel to match the controller's voltage and
   current limits.
2. Fuse every source and use a disconnect at the battery.
3. Use cable rated for the current and UV exposure; crimp and seal connectors.
4. Ground the array frame and equipment according to local code.

### 4. Commission and monitor

1. Check polarity and open-circuit voltage before connecting the controller.
2. Connect the battery first if the controller requires it, then the array.
3. Verify charging current and battery voltage in sun and shade.
4. Record daily output and inspect terminals for corrosion every few months.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** PV panels produce dangerous DC voltage whenever light falls
  on them. Cover them and isolate before wiring.
- Batteries can release hydrogen and acid. Ventilate, wear eye protection, and
  avoid sparks.
- Undersized cable and missing fuses cause fires. Size for continuous current
  and fault current.
- Work on roofs with fall protection; do not work alone.

title: Solar Thermal
body:
## Overview

Solar thermal collects sunlight as heat — for cooking, water heating,
sterilization, and drying. Simpler and cheaper than photovoltaics.

## Prerequisites

- [Simple Tools](../survival/simple-tools.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Reflective surface (mirror, foil, polished metal)
- Absorber (black metal)
- Insulation
- Glass or plastic cover
- Water pipes (for heaters)

## Procedure

### Solar Cooker (Box Type)

1. Build a wooden box 50 × 50 × 30 cm.
2. Line with insulation (straw, newspaper).
3. Blacken the interior base.
4. Glass lid on top.
5. Reflector flap angled to direct sunlight.
6. Temp: 120–150°C. Cooks rice in 2 hours.

### Parabolic Cooker

1. Satellite dish lined with Mylar or mirror strips.
2. Focus point holds a black pot.
3. Temp: 250–400°C. Cooks as fast as a stove.
4. Must be adjusted every 15 minutes.

### Solar Water Heater (Batch)

1. Black tank (50–100 L) in an insulated box with glass top.
2. Cold water enters bottom; hot exits top.
3. Temp: 60–80°C on sunny days.

### Solar Water Heater (Thermosiphon)

1. Flat plate collector: black absorber + copper pipes + glass cover.
2. Tank above collector; thermosiphon circulates water.
3. More efficient than batch.

### Solar Still

1. Pit with black liner.
2. Salty or dirty water in the pit.
3. Glass or plastic cover slopes to a collection channel.
4. Yield: 1–4 L/m²/day.

### Solar Dryer

1. Box with black interior and glass top.
2. Chimney for airflow.
3. Dries fruit, vegetables, meat in 1–3 days.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Parabolic cookers reach 400°C — fires and burns.
  Use gloves, never leave unattended.
- Never look directly at concentrated sunlight.
- Solar cookers work poorly in clouds; have a backup.

title: Wind Power
body:
## Overview

Wind turbines convert kinetic energy into electricity or mechanical power.
Small turbines (1–10 kW) can charge batteries or pump water.

## Prerequisites

- [Simple Tools](../survival/simple-tools.md)
- [Electrical Wiring](electrical-wiring.md)
- [Battery Basics](battery-basics.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Blades (wood, fiberglass, or PVC pipe)
- Generator (permanent magnet alternator)
- Tower or mast
- Guy wires
- Charge controller
- Batteries

## Procedure

### Sizing

1. Measure average wind speed at hub height.
2. Power ∝ (wind speed)³ × (rotor area).
3. 1 m diameter rotor ≈ 30 W at 5 m/s; 3 m ≈ 300 W; 5 m ≈ 1 kW.

### Blade Design

1. 3 blades preferred (balance of torque and speed).
2. Tapered and twisted for efficiency.
3. Tip speed ratio (TSR): 5–7 for electricity, 2–3 for water pumping.
4. Pitch: 10–20° at the root, 0° at the tip.

### Alternator (Axial Flux PMG)

1. Two steel disks with magnets (N-S alternating).
2. Stator with coils between them.
3. 3-phase output rectified to DC.
4. Example: 12 magnets, 9 coils → 12 V at 300 RPM.

### Tower

1. Height: 10 m minimum for small turbines.
2. Guy wires at 3 levels.
3. Furling mechanism (tail vane) for overspeed protection.

### Electrical

1. Rectify 3-phase AC → DC.
2. Charge controller prevents overcharge.
3. Dump load (resistor) for excess.
4. Inverter for AC loads.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Blades spin at 300+ RPM — decapitation risk.
- Never touch a spinning rotor.
- Guy wires under tension snap — stay clear.
- Turbine must be furled or braked in storms.
- Lightning protection required.

title: Wood Gasification
body:
## Overview

Gasification converts wood into combustible gas (CO + H₂ + CH₄) that can
power engines, generators, and stoves.

## Prerequisites

- [Charcoal Production](../materials/charcoal-production.md)
- [Fire & Combustion](fire-combustion.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Gasifier (downdraft or updraft)
- Wood chips or pellets
- Pipes (steel)
- Filter (cyclone + fabric)
- Cooler

## Procedure

### Downdraft Gasifier

1. Build a steel reactor 60 cm tall, 20 cm diameter.
2. Air inlet at top.
3. Throat (constriction) at ⅓ height.
4. Combustion zone: 900–1,100°C.
5. Reduction zone below: 700–900°C produces CO and H₂.

### Feedstock

- Wood chips 2–5 cm, moisture <20%
- Avoid bark and leaves (tar and ash).
- Pelletize fines for uniform feed.

### Gas Cleaning

1. **Cyclone:** removes large particles.
2. **Cooler:** drops temp to <50°C.
3. **Fabric filter:** removes remaining particles.
4. **Optional scrubber:** water or oil for tar.

### Using the Gas

- **Generator:** modify spark-ignition engine (petrol) with gas mixer.
- **Stove:** direct burn with secondary air.
- **Boiler:** fire into combustion chamber.

### Efficiency

- 1 kg wood → 2.5–3 Nm³ gas → ~5 MJ energy.
- 20–25% of wood energy becomes usable gas.
- Char and heat are byproducts.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Producer gas is 20–30% CO — highly toxic, odorless.
  Never operate indoors. Use CO detectors.
- Gas is explosive in air (12–75% range). No sparks.
- Tar clogs pipes and engines; maintain cleaning schedule.
- Do not inhale gas while lighting; use a torch on a stick.

title: Anatomy Basics
body:
## Overview

Knowing the body's systems and landmarks guides examination, first aid, and referral. Focus on the skeleton, major vessels, organs, and the airway.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Anatomical charts (public domain)
- Notebook
- Skeleton model (optional)

## Procedure

### Systems Overview

1. Learn the skeletal, muscular, circulatory, respiratory, digestive, and nervous systems.
2. Memorize the positions of the heart, lungs, liver, spleen, and kidneys.

### Landmarks

1. Palpate pulse points: radial, carotid, femoral.
2. Identify the airway, cricoid, and sternal notch.

## Safety Notes

- Anatomy knowledge supports, but does not replace, trained care.

title: Antibiotics

sources.title: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines

body:
## Overview

Antibiotics cure bacterial infection. Knowing which drug for which bug, and completing the full course, prevents resistance and relapse.

## Prerequisites

- Wound Care

## Materials & Tools

- Antibiotic stocks
- Clean water
- Dosing chart

## Procedure

### Selection

1. Match drug to likely organism and site.
2. Prefer narrow-spectrum agents when the target is known.

### Administration

1. Give the full course at correct intervals and dose.
2. Adjust for weight, age, pregnancy, and kidney function.

### Resistance

1. Never use antibiotics for viral illness.
2. Rotate and reserve drugs to slow resistance.

## Safety Notes

- Red hazard: allergies (especially penicillin) can be fatal.
- Overuse breeds resistant organisms that threaten the whole community.

title: Childbirth

sources.title: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth

body:
## Overview

Most births need only patience, warmth, cleanliness, and support. Recognizing obstructed labor and hemorrhage prevents the two leading causes of maternal death.

## Prerequisites

- Anatomy Basics

## Materials & Tools

- Clean cloths
- Sterile scissors or blade
- Cord ties
- Warm, clean space

## Procedure

### Labor Support

1. Keep the mother warm, hydrated, and calm.
2. Monitor contractions and the baby's descent.

### Delivery

1. Support the perineum and deliver the head slowly.
2. Check for a cord around the neck and clear the airway.
3. Deliver the body, then clamp and cut the cord.

### Aftercare

1. Deliver the placenta and watch for heavy bleeding.
2. Keep mother and newborn warm and begin breastfeeding.

## Safety Notes

- Red hazard: heavy bleeding, fever, or prolonged labor requires skilled help.
- Uterotonic medication and manual pressure control postpartum hemorrhage.

title: Dental Care
body:
## Overview

Dental pain disables and dental infection can spread fatally. Prevention by cleaning and diet comes first; extraction is the reliable field cure.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Toothbrush or chew stick
- Fluoride or salt
- Dental instruments

## Procedure

### Prevention

1. Brush or chew clean sticks after meals.
2. Limit sugar; encourage fibrous foods.

### Pain & Abscess

1. Apply cold compresses and analgesics.
2. Drain a fluctuant abscess and give antibiotics if systemic.

### Extraction

1. Numb the area and loosen the tooth with elevators.
2. Remove smoothly, then pack the socket for a clean clot.

## Safety Notes

- Never extract an infected tooth with airway involvement; refer urgently.
- Manage bleeding and shock after extraction.

title: Field Diagnostics
body:
## Overview

Without a laboratory, diagnosis relies on history, vital signs, and physical examination. A structured approach separates emergencies from routine illness.

## Prerequisites

- Anatomy Basics

## Materials & Tools

- Thermometer
- Clock or watch
- Blood-pressure cuff
- Flashlight

## Procedure

### History & Vitals

1. Record onset, duration, and severity of symptoms.
2. Measure temperature, pulse, respiration, and blood pressure.

### Examination

1. Inspect, palpate, percuss, and auscultate each system.
2. Check for dehydration, pallor, and level of consciousness.

### Triage

1. Sort into immediate, delayed, and expectant categories.
2. Reassess regularly; conditions change quickly.

## Safety Notes

- Isolate patients with suspected airborne infection.
- Refer unknown or worsening cases to the most skilled caregiver available.

title: Field Surgery
body:
## Overview

Field surgery addresses life-threatening injuries when evacuation is impossible. Sterile technique, anesthesia, and hemorrhage control are mandatory prerequisites.

## Prerequisites

- Wound Care
- Anatomy Basics

## Materials & Tools

- Sterile instruments
- Anesthetic
- Suture and needles
- Antibiotics

## Procedure

### Preparation

1. Stabilize airway, breathing, and circulation first.
2. Sterilize instruments by boiling or autoclaving.
3. Clean and drape the surgical field.

### Operate

1. Control bleeding with clamps and ligatures.
2. Debride non-viable tissue and remove foreign bodies.
3. Repair structures and close in layers where appropriate.

### Aftercare

1. Give analgesics and antibiotics.
2. Monitor for shock, infection, and bleeding.

## Safety Notes

- Red hazard: only perform when trained and when death is otherwise certain.
- Maintain sterile technique or the operation will cost more lives than it saves.

title: Mental Health
body:
## Overview

Disaster and isolation cause acute stress, grief, and depression. Safety, connection, routine, and dignity are the first-line treatments.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Quiet space
- Water and food
- Daily routine plan

## Procedure

### Psychological First Aid

1. Ensure safety and basic needs.
2. Listen without judgment; do not force retelling.
3. Connect people to family and community.

### Ongoing Support

1. Establish routine, sleep, and physical activity.
2. Offer meaningful work and social roles.
3. Refer severe cases with risk of self-harm for specialist care.

## Safety Notes

- Never leave someone at acute risk of self-harm alone.
- Avoid debriefing that forces recounting of trauma.

title: Mass Casualty Triage
storage: Keep triage tags and kits stocked and inspect them every 3 months
hazards: Missed internal bleeding or airway obstruction

sources.title: START Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment
NATO Emergency War Surgery triage chapter

body:
## Overview

Triage sorts injured people by urgency when demand exceeds resources. It is not
a diagnosis: it is a repeated, rapid decision about who needs treatment first
and who can wait. The goal is to do the greatest good for the greatest number,
not to treat the most dramatic injury first.

## Prerequisites

- Basic first aid
- A practised triage method and clear roles

## Materials & Tools

- Colour-coded triage tags
- Permanent markers
- Gloves and eye protection
- Headlamp
- Bandages and tourniquets
- Clipboard and tally sheet
- Radio or runner system

## Procedure

### 1. Make the scene safe

1. Stop and assess hazards: traffic, fire, structural collapse, violence.
2. Do not become a casualty; wait for the scene to be secured if needed.
3. Identify a triage officer and a treatment area away from the hazard.
4. Establish one-way flow: triage, treatment, transport.

### 2. Triage each casualty

1. Use a rapid method such as START: check ability to walk, breathing,
   perfusion, and mental status.
2. Tag immediate (red) for life threats needing treatment within minutes,
   delayed (yellow) for serious but stable, minor (green) for walking wounded,
   and deceased (black) after confirmation.
3. Control catastrophic bleeding with direct pressure or a tourniquet during
   the primary sweep.
4. Spend no more than 30-60 seconds per casualty in the initial triage.

### 3. Reassess and treat

1. Re-triage after movement or deterioration; tags are not permanent.
2. Treat red casualties in order of likely benefit, not arrival order.
3. Keep airways open, stop bleeding, and prevent hypothermia.
4. Record identity, tag colour, time, and interventions.

### 4. Transport and communicate

1. Match transport priority to triage colour and destination capability.
2. Send a tally of casualties to the receiving facility.
3. Keep families informed through a single, trusted source.
4. Debrief the response and rest the team in shifts.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Triage errors cost lives. Practise and use a recognised
  method.
- Use gloves and eye protection; assume all blood and body fluids are
  infectious.
- Do not enter an unstable structure or an active threat scene.
- Psychological stress is cumulative. Rotate roles and provide support.

title: Wound Care
body:
## Overview

Prompt cleaning and dressing prevents infection, the leading killer of field wounds. Control bleeding, remove debris, and keep the wound moist and covered.

## Prerequisites

- Basic First Aid

## Materials & Tools

- Clean water
- Soap
- Dressing and bandage
- Honey or antiseptic

## Procedure

### Cleaning

1. Control bleeding with direct pressure.
2. Irrigate the wound with clean, preferably boiled, water.
3. Remove visible dirt and dead tissue.

### Dressing

1. Apply a thin layer of honey or antiseptic for superficial wounds.
2. Cover with a clean non-stick dressing and change daily.

### Monitoring

1. Watch for spreading redness, pus, fever, or foul smell.
2. Escalate to antibiotic treatment if infection develops.

## Safety Notes

- Never close a contaminated or bite wound tightly.
- Tetanus prevention matters for all puncture wounds.

title: Bookbinding and Repair
yield: 1-20 books per day depending on binding style and drying time
season: Any; keep glue and paper dry
storage: Store finished books upright, dry, and out of direct sun
hazards: Mould if books are stored damp

sources.title: Library of Congress Book Repair Guidelines

body:
## Overview

Books survive only if their binding is repaired before pages are lost. Simple
pamphlet stitching, case binding, and spine repair need few tools and can be
taught quickly. A binder can produce 1-20 books a day depending on style,
drying time, and how much work is repair rather than new binding.

## Prerequisites

- Paper making or access to suitable paper
- Basic hand-tool skills

## Materials & Tools

- Paper signatures
- Linen thread and wax
- Book cloth or leather
- Binder's board
- PVA or cooked starch paste
- Endpapers
- Bone folder, awl, needle, and knife
- Book press or weighted boards

## Procedure

### 1. Prepare the text block

1. Fold sheets into signatures with the grain running vertically.
2. Collate pages in order and check for missing or reversed sheets.
3. Press the folded signatures overnight to flatten the folds.
4. Mark sewing stations along the spine with an awl.

### 2. Sew the book

1. Sew through the stations with waxed linen thread; keep tension even.
2. Link each signature to the previous one so the block holds together.
3. Tie off securely and press the sewn block.
4. Glue the spine with a flexible adhesive and line it with cloth or paper.

### 3. Make the case

1. Cut two boards and a spine strip to size, allowing a small square at the
   edges.
2. Cover the boards with cloth or leather, working from the centre outward.
3. Turn in the edges neatly and press the case flat.
4. Attach the text block with endpapers, keeping the spine flexible.

### 4. Repair and protect

1. Tighten loose hinges with a thin line of PVA and press.
2. Repair torn pages with Japanese tissue and starch paste.
3. Reback a broken spine with new cloth, not household tape.
4. Store upright, dry, and out of direct sun; keep pests away.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Knives and awls cause deep puncture wounds. Cut away from
  the body and keep tools sharp.
- Use glue in a ventilated area; solvent-based adhesives are toxic.
- Repetitive folding and sewing strain hands and wrists; take breaks.
- Damp books grow mould. Dry wet books immediately and separate pages.

title: Cryptography
body:
## Overview

Cryptography protects messages and identity when channels are insecure. One-time pads give unbreakable secrecy; hashes verify integrity.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- One-time pad tables
- Pencil and paper
- Checksum tables

## Procedure

### One-Time Pad

1. Generate truly random key material equal in length to the message.
2. Add key to plaintext mod 26 to encrypt; subtract to decrypt.
3. Destroy each key after one use.

### Integrity

1. Append a hash or checksum to detect tampering.
2. Verify with a shared secret where possible.

## Safety Notes

- Never reuse a one-time pad; reuse makes it breakable.
- Protect keys as carefully as the message.

title: Education
body:
## Overview

Education transmits skills and values across generations. A curriculum built on literacy, numeracy, and apprenticeship rebuilds capability quickly.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Slates or paper
- Curriculum outline
- Trained instructors

## Procedure

### Foundations

1. Teach reading and writing first, then arithmetic.
2. Use local materials, stories, and practical problems.

### Apprenticeship

1. Pair learners with skilled practitioners.
2. Progress from observation to supervised work to independent practice.

### Assessment

1. Check understanding with practical tasks.
2. Adjust instruction to close gaps.

## Safety Notes

- Safeguard children; keep learning environments safe and inclusive.

title: Library Organization
body:
## Overview

An organized library keeps knowledge findable for generations. A simple classification plus a catalog protects against loss and makes retrieval fast.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Shelving
- Catalog cards or ledger
- Labels and ink

## Procedure

### Classification

1. Group by broad subject, then by author or title.
2. Assign a stable call number to every item.

### Catalog

1. Record title, author, subject, and location for each item.
2. Maintain an index for cross-referencing.

### Preservation

1. Keep collections dry, dark, and pest-free.
2. Copy fragile items and store masters separately.

## Safety Notes

- Control humidity and fire risk; back up catalogs.

title: Measurement & Records
body:
## Overview

Consistent measurement and record-keeping make knowledge reproducible. Standard units, calibrated references, and ledgers underpin trade and science.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Standard weights and measures
- Ledger or logbook
- Calibration references

## Procedure

### Standards

1. Adopt units for length, mass, volume, and time.
2. Keep master references under protection.

### Records

1. Log observations with date, method, and conditions.
2. Cross-reference entries for auditability.

## Safety Notes

- Guard standards against wear and tampering.

title: Music
body:
## Overview

Music is a universal human language. It binds communities, transmits stories,
and heals trauma. Instruments can be built from local materials.

## Prerequisites

- [Simple Tools](../survival/simple-tools.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Wood, gut, hide, bamboo, gourd
- Metal (for strings, bells)
- Voice

## Procedure

### Rhythm First

1. Clapping patterns: 4/4, 3/4, 6/8.
2. Call and response.
3. Polyrhythms: two patterns at once.

### Drums

- **Frame drum:** hide stretched over a wooden hoop.
- **Djembe:** goblet-shaped, rope-tuned.
- **Log drum:** hollowed log with slits.

### Jaw Harp

1. Shape a metal or bamboo tongue in a frame.
2. Pluck the tongue while changing mouth shape.
3. Mouth cavity amplifies harmonics.

### Flutes

- **Bamboo flute:** cut a tube, bore finger holes, notch the mouthpiece.
- **Pan pipes:** graduated tubes bound together.
- **Ocarina:** closed vessel with finger holes.

### String Instruments

- **Berimbau:** bow with a gourd resonator.
- **Lyre:** U-shaped frame with strings.
- **Guitar:** box with neck and frets.

### Music Theory (Basic)

1. **Scale:** 7 notes per octave (do re mi fa sol la ti).
2. **Intervals:** distance between notes.
3. **Chords:** three or more notes together.
4. **Keys:** major (bright), minor (dark).

### Singing

1. Breathe from the diaphragm.
2. Open the throat.
3. Match pitch with an instrument.
4. Sing in rounds, harmonies, and unison.

### Songs for Community

- Work songs (rhythm for shared labor).
- Lullabies.
- Lamentations.
- Celebration songs.
- Anthems.

### Recording (If Available)

- Wax cylinder, magnetic tape, or digital.
- Preserve for future generations.

## Safety Notes

- Green — but loud sounds damage hearing. Protect ears around drums.
- Singing is safe; hydrate.

title: Optics
body:
## Overview

Optics magnify, focus, and direct light, enabling reading aids, telescopes, microscopes, and fire-starting. Grinding and polishing produce lenses from glass.

## Prerequisites

- Glass Making

## Materials & Tools

- Glass blanks
- Abrasives and pitch
- Polishing rouge

## Procedure

### Grinding

1. Rough-grind the blank against a tool with coarse abrasive.
2. Progress to finer abrasives until the curve is correct.

### Polishing

1. Polish on pitch with rouge until clear.
2. Test focus on a bright object.

### Use

1. Combine lenses into a telescope or microscope.
2. Focus sunlight for ignition.

## Safety Notes

- Never view the sun directly through optics; it causes blindness.
- Focused sunlight can start fires instantly.

title: Oral History
body:
## Overview

When writing is scarce, oral history preserves memory, law, and craft. Structured interviews and mnemonic devices keep it accurate.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Notebook or recording device
- Question guides
- Storytellers

## Procedure

### Collecting

1. Interview elders with open questions and permission.
2. Record exact wording and context.

### Preserving

1. Transcribe and cross-check with other accounts.
2. Teach key stories to younger people through repetition and song.

## Safety Notes

- Obtain consent and respect cultural ownership of stories.

title: Printing
body:
## Overview

Printing spreads knowledge cheaply and durably. Movable type, an oil ink, and a screw press let a small community reproduce books and posters.

## Prerequisites

- Paper Making

## Materials & Tools

- Movable metal or wooden type
- Oil-based ink
- Screw press
- Paper

## Procedure

### Making Type

1. Carve or cast reversed letters at a uniform height.
2. Sort type into a case by frequency.

### Setting & Inking

1. Compose text in a galley, locked into a forme.
2. Ink the forme evenly with leather balls or a roller.

### Pressing

1. Lay paper, close the tympan, and run the press.
2. Hang sheets to dry; print the second side after drying.

## Safety Notes

- Ink and solvent fumes require ventilation.
- Keep hands clear of the press platen.

title: Radio

sources.title: US Army Signal Corps manuals (public domain)

body:
## Overview

Radio links communities beyond line of sight, using no infrastructure. A simple crystal set receives; a low-power transceiver sends voice or Morse.

## Prerequisites

- Electrical Wiring

## Materials & Tools

- Copper wire
- Variable capacitor and coil
- Crystal earpiece or diode
- Antenna wire

## Procedure

### Receiver

1. Wind a coil and connect it to a variable capacitor to tune.
2. Add a diode detector and crystal earpiece.
3. Connect a long wire antenna and a good earth.

### Antenna

1. Run a half-wave dipole as high and clear as possible.
2. Feed with twin lead or coax and seal connections.

### Transmission

1. Use low power and a licensed band.
2. Send Morse or voice; identify your station.

## Safety Notes

- Powerful transmitters and antennas can cause RF burns and shocks.
- Follow local spectrum rules and keep emergency frequencies clear.

title: Blacksmithing
body:
## Overview

Blacksmithing shapes wrought iron and steel by heating and hammering. It
produces tools, weapons, hardware, and fasteners.

## Prerequisites

- [Charcoal Production](charcoal-production.md)
- [Metal Smelting](metal-smelting.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Forge (clay or steel)
- Anvil (or dense stone)
- Hammer (2–4 kg)
- Tongs
- Quench tank (oil or water)
- Charcoal

## Procedure

### Setting Up the Forge

1. Build a clay hearth with a tuyere at the center.
2. Connect bellows or blower.
3. Fill with charcoal; light from the top.
4. Air blast raises temp to 1,200–1,400°C.

### Basic Forging

1. Heat metal to bright orange-yellow (1,100°C).
2. Remove; hammer immediately.
3. Reheat as it turns cherry red (below 800°C).
4. Shape by drawing, upsetting, bending, or punching.

### Drawing Out

1. Heat a section.
2. Hammer on the anvil's horn or face, striking perpendicular to length.
3. Rotate 90° between blows to keep square.

### Upsetting

1. Heat the end.
2. Strike downward onto the anvil; thickness increases, length shortens.

### Welding (Forge Weld)

1. Heat both pieces to white-yellow (1,300°C).
2. Sprinkle borax as flux.
3. Overlap; hammer rapidly. The pieces fuse.

### Heat Treatment

1. **Annealing:** heat to red, cool slowly in ash.
2. **Normalizing:** heat to red, air-cool.
3. **Hardening:** heat to red, quench in oil or water.
4. **Tempering:** reheat to 200–300°C (straw to purple color), then cool.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Burns, eye injuries, and hearing damage are common.
- Wear leather apron, eye protection, ear protection.
- Never quench in water without knowing the steel — cracking risk.
- Keep water away from the forge unless intentional.
- Ventilate for CO.

title: Brick Making
materialsRequired: Clay (test: rolls into a smooth snake without cracking)
body:
## Overview

Bricks are clay fired to hardness. They are the backbone of durable
construction — houses, kilns, furnaces, chimneys.

## Prerequisites

- [Making Fire](../survival/making-fire.md)
- [Charcoal Production](charcoal-production.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Clay (test: rolls into a smooth snake without cracking)
- Sand (temper)
- Water
- Wooden molds
- Kiln or clamp

## Procedure

### Clay Preparation

1. Dig clay; remove rocks and roots.
2. Add sand (10–20% by volume) to reduce shrinkage.
3. Add water; knead to plastic consistency.
4. Let rest 24 hours (aging improves workability).

### Molding

1. Wet mold; dust with sand.
2. Press clay firmly into mold.
3. Strike off excess with a board.
4. Turn out onto a drying board.

### Drying

1. Air-dry in shade 1–2 weeks.
2. Turn daily to prevent warping.
3. Bone-dry before firing (no moisture).

### Firing

1. Build a clamp: stack bricks with gaps for fire.
2. Cover with mud; leave air channels at base.
3. Fire slowly for 24 hours; peak at 900–1,000°C.
4. Cool 2 days before opening.

### Testing

- Fired brick rings when struck.
- Underfired brick is dull and crumbles.
- Overfired brick is glassy and vitrified (good for kilns).

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Silica dust in clay — wear mask when dry mixing.
- Firing clamp releases smoke and CO — keep away from dwellings.
- Do not use bricks from unknown sources for food-contact surfaces.

title: Charcoal Production
body:
## Overview

Charcoal burns hotter and cleaner than wood and is essential for smelting
and blacksmithing. It is made by pyrolysis — burning wood with limited oxygen.

## Prerequisites

- [Making Fire](../survival/making-fire.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Hardwood (oak, hickory, mesquite)
- Earth or sand
- Shovel
- Water (for quenching)

## Procedure

### Earth Kiln Method

1. Clear a 2 m circle; level the ground.
2. Stack hardwood in a dome, leaving a central chimney.
3. Cover the pile with leaves, then earth, leaving the chimney open.
4. Light the chimney.
5. When smoke turns from white to blue, close the chimney.
6. Tend for 3–7 days, patching cracks as they appear.
7. When smoke stops, wait 24 hours; then open and quench with water.

### Retort Method (Higher Yield)

1. Place wood in a sealed metal drum.
2. Heat from outside; volatile gases escape via a pipe.
3. Those gases can fuel the fire — self-sustaining once started.
4. Cool before opening.

### Yield

- Earth kiln: 10–20% by weight
- Retort: 25–35%

### Uses

- Smelting iron, copper
- Blacksmithing forges
- Water filtration (activated charcoal)
- Gunpowder (see [Chemistry](chemistry.md))
- Medicinal (charcoal slurry for poisoning)

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Carbon monoxide from smoldering charcoal kills without warning. Work outdoors.
- Never seal a drum while hot — pressure builds.
- Quench thoroughly; buried embers can reignite days later.

title: Chemistry
materialsRequired: Acids: vinegar (acetic), citric (lemon), sulfuric (from sulfide ores)
Bases: lime (CaO), wood ash (K₂CO₃), ammonia (from urine)
body:
## Overview

Chemistry underpins soap, medicine, metallurgy, and agriculture. This entry
covers the foundational reactions and safety rules needed to produce acids,
bases, salts, and simple organic compounds.

## Prerequisites

- [Metal Smelting](metal-smelting.md)
- [Charcoal Production](charcoal-production.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Glass vessels (see [Glass Making](glass-making.md))
- Heat source (charcoal forge)
- Acids: vinegar (acetic), citric (lemon), sulfuric (from sulfide ores)
- Bases: lime (CaO), wood ash (K₂CO₃), ammonia (from urine)
- Litmus or red cabbage indicator

## Procedure

### Safety First

1. Always add acid to water, never water to acid.
2. Wear eye protection and gloves.
3. Work outdoors or under a fume hood.
4. Have a bucket of water and baking soda within reach.

### Making Sulfuric Acid (Lead Chamber)

1. Burn sulfur in a lead-lined chamber with moist air.
2. SO₂ + O₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.
3. Collect the acid at the chamber base.
4. Concentrate by boiling off water.

### Making Nitric Acid (Saltpeter + Sulfuric)

1. Mix saltpeter (KNO₃) with sulfuric acid in a glass retort.
2. Heat gently; distill nitric acid into a cooled receiver.
3. Store in dark glass.

### Making Hydrochloric Acid (Salt + Sulfuric)

1. Mix table salt with sulfuric acid.
2. Collect HCl gas in water.
3. Store in glass.

### Making Lye (Potassium Hydroxide)

1. Leach hardwood ash with rainwater.
2. Evaporate to concentrate.
3. Test with a fresh egg — it floats when strong enough.

### Making Soap (Saponification)

See [Soap Making](../survival/soap-making.md).

### Making Gunpowder

1. Mix 75% potassium nitrate, 15% charcoal, 10% sulfur by weight.
2. Mill to a fine powder.
3. **Red hazard:** Static sparks ignite powder. Work with wooden tools, ground yourself.

### pH Testing (Red Cabbage Indicator)

1. Boil red cabbage; save the purple liquid.
2. Add a drop of test solution.
3. Red = acid, green = base, purple = neutral.

### Common Reactions

- **Neutralization:** acid + base → salt + water.
- **Oxidation:** metal + oxygen → oxide.
- **Reduction:** oxide + carbon → metal + CO₂.
- **Combustion:** fuel + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Concentrated acids and bases destroy tissue on contact.
- **Red hazard:** Many reactions produce toxic or explosive gases.
- Never taste or smell chemicals directly.
- Never store acids in metal containers.
- Ventilate always.

title: Glass Making
materialsRequired: Soda ash (from burnt kelp or natron)
body:
## Overview

Glass is made from silica (sand), soda ash, and lime, melted at 1,400°C.
It is essential for windows, lenses, containers, and labware.

## Prerequisites

- [Charcoal Production](charcoal-production.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Silica sand (white, clean)
- Soda ash (from burnt kelp or natron)
- Lime (from limestone)
- Crucible (clay)
- Blowpipe
- Annealing oven

## Procedure

### Glass Batch

1. Mix by weight: 70% silica, 15% soda ash, 10% lime, 5% cullet (recycled glass).
2. Grind to powder; mix thoroughly.

### Melting

1. Heat crucible in furnace to 1,400°C.
2. Add batch slowly; it will foam as CO₂ escapes.
3. Skim off impurities.
4. Hold at 1,200°C for working.

### Blowing

1. Dip blowpipe in molten glass; gather a gob.
2. Roll on a marver (metal plate) to shape.
3. Blow gently through the pipe; rotate continuously.
4. Shape with jacks (tongs) and a wooden paddle.
5. Transfer to a punty rod for the open end.

### Annealing

1. Place finished glass in an oven at 500°C.
2. Cool slowly (1°C/min) to room temperature.
3. Rapid cooling causes shattering.

### Flat Glass (Cylinder Method)

1. Blow a large cylinder.
2. Cut off ends; slit lengthwise.
3. Reheat and flatten in an oven.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Molten glass causes severe burns and sticks to skin.
- Furnace gases (CO, SO₂) are toxic — ventilate.
- Silica dust causes silicosis — wear respirator when mixing batch.
- Never quench hot glass in water.

title: Leather Tanning
body:
## Overview

Tanning stabilizes animal hide against rot. Methods: vegetable (bark),
brain, alum, and chrome. Vegetable is the safest and most traditional.

## Prerequisites

- [Raising Livestock](../agriculture/raising-livestock.md)
- [Simple Tools](../survival/simple-tools.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Fresh hide
- Bark (oak, chestnut, mimosa — high tannin)
- Lime (for dehairing)
- Fleshing knife
- Tanning vat
- Wooden beam

## Procedure

### Fleshing

1. Soak the hide in water 1–2 days.
2. Lay over a beam; scrape flesh and fat with a dull knife.
3. Remove hair by soaking in lime water (pH 12) 1–2 weeks.
4. Scrape hair and epidermis.

### Deliming & Bating

1. Rinse in water.
2. Soak in a weak acid (vinegar or bran water) 1 day to neutralize lime.
3. Bate (soften) in a warm manure or enzyme solution 1–3 days.

### Vegetable Tanning

1. Build a series of vats with increasing tannin concentration.
2. Start with weak "spent" tan liquor (1:10 bark to water).
3. Move the hide through stronger liquors over 4–12 weeks.
4. Finish in a strong tan pit 1–4 weeks.
5. When fully tanned (uniform brown throughout), remove.

### Brain Tanning (Native American Method)

1. Every animal has enough brain to tan its own hide.
2. Mash brain with water; work into the hide.
3. Stretch and dry; work with hands and a rope to soften.

### Finishing

1. Rinse.
2. Oil with tallow or fish oil.
3. Stretch and dry slowly.
4. Work with a slicker and stake to soften.
5. Smoke over a smoldering fire for color and water resistance.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Lime burns skin; wear gloves and eye protection.
- Raw hides carry zoonotic diseases (anthrax, brucellosis) — handle with care.
- Tanning solutions smell; work outdoors, away from dwellings.

title: Lime & Cement

sources.title: US Bureau of Mines cement reports

body:
## Overview

Lime and cement are binders for masonry and concrete. Lime comes from
limestone (CaCO₃) burned to quicklime (CaO). Cement adds silica and alumina.

## Prerequisites

- [Brick Making](brick-making.md)
- [Charcoal Production](charcoal-production.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Limestone or chalk
- Kiln
- Water
- Sand, gravel (aggregate)
- Pozzolan (volcanic ash or fired clay)

## Procedure

### Lime Burning

1. Crush limestone to 5 cm pieces.
2. Fill kiln; fire to 900–1,000°C for 12–24 hours.
3. Quicklime (CaO) results — highly caustic.
4. Store in sealed containers away from moisture.

### Slaking

1. Slowly add water to quicklime (violent exotherm).
2. Result is slaked lime (Ca(OH)₂) — putty or powder.
3. Let mature 1–4 weeks before use.

### Lime Mortar

1. Mix 1 part lime putty to 3 parts sand.
2. Add water to workable consistency.
3. Use within 2 hours.
4. Cures by carbonation (absorbs CO₂) — slow, months.

### Hydraulic Lime

1. Limestone with 10–20% clay fires to hydraulic lime.
2. Sets underwater — useful for foundations and cisterns.

### Roman Cement (Pozzolanic)

1. Mix slaked lime with pozzolan (volcanic ash) 2:1.
2. Add sand and aggregate.
3. Sets hard underwater — used in aqueducts and harbors.

### Portland Cement (Modern)

1. Burn limestone + clay at 1,450°C to clinker.
2. Grind clinker with 5% gypsum to powder.
3. Mix with sand, gravel, water (1:2:3 by volume) for concrete.
4. Cure 28 days for full strength.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Quicklime burns skin and eyes on contact; slaking releases
  boiling water. Wear full PPE.
- Cement dust causes silicosis and chemical burns — respirator, gloves.
- Never add water to cement in a confined space (heat and steam).

title: Metal Smelting
materialsRequired: Ore (malachite for copper; hematite/magnetite for iron)
body:
## Overview

Smelting extracts metal from ore using heat and a reducing agent (charcoal).
Start with copper (1,085°C), then bronze (alloy), then iron (1,538°C).

## Prerequisites

- [Charcoal Production](charcoal-production.md)
- [Simple Tools](../survival/simple-tools.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Ore (malachite for copper; hematite/magnetite for iron)
- Charcoal
- Clay furnace or bloomery
- Bellows
- Hammer and anvil

## Procedure

### Finding Ore

- **Copper:** green-stained rocks (malachite, azurite).
- **Iron:** red-brown rocks (hematite), magnetic black sand (magnetite).
- **Lead:** galena (gray cubic crystals).
- **Tin:** cassiterite (heavy black grains in stream beds).

### Building a Furnace

1. Build a clay cylinder 50 cm tall, 30 cm diameter.
2. Add a tuyere (air pipe) at the base for bellows.
3. Line with clay; let dry slowly.

### Copper Smelting

1. Crush ore to 1 cm pieces.
2. Layer charcoal and ore in furnace.
3. Light; pump bellows continuously.
4. After 45 min, tap slag; collect molten copper at base.
5. Yield: 5–20% copper by ore weight.

### Iron Bloomery

1. Same furnace, taller (1 m).
2. Alternate charcoal and crushed iron ore.
3. Pump bellows for 4–6 hours.
4. Extract a "bloom" — spongy iron mixed with slag.
5. Hammer the bloom while hot to expel slag (wrought iron).

### Bronze (Alloy)

1. Melt copper (1,085°C).
2. Add tin (10–12% by weight).
3. Cast into molds. Bronze is harder than copper and easier to cast.

### Cast Iron

1. Higher carbon content (2–4%).
2. Requires higher temp (1,200°C+) and continuous blast.
3. Brittle but hard; cast into shapes.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Molten metal causes severe burns. Wear leather and eye protection.
- Metal fumes (lead, zinc, arsenic) are toxic — ventilate.
- Never pour molten metal onto wet surfaces (steam explosion).
- Carbon monoxide from charcoal — work outdoors.

title: Mills
materialsRequired: Wood for frame, gears, and wheel
body:
## Overview

Mills grind grain, press oil, saw wood, and full cloth. They are powered by
water, wind, or animals. Mills are force multipliers for any community.

## Prerequisites

- [Simple Tools](../survival/simple-tools.md)
- [Rope & Cordage](../survival/rope-cordage.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Millstones (hard granite or basalt)
- Wood for frame, gears, and wheel
- Metal bearings and shafts (see [Blacksmithing](blacksmithing.md))
- Water source or wind exposure

## Procedure

### Water Mill (Undershot)

1. Site on a stream with year-round flow.
2. Build a wheel 2–4 m diameter with paddles.
3. Mount on a horizontal axle; support with wooden or metal bearings.
4. Couple to millstone via gears (see [Mechanics](../materials/mechanics.md)).
5. Build a sluice to direct water onto the paddles.

### Water Mill (Overshot — More Efficient)

1. Build a flume to carry water over the top of the wheel.
2. Wheel has buckets instead of paddles.
3. Water weight drives the wheel downward.

### Windmill

1. Tower 6–12 m tall with a rotating top (cap).
2. Sails: 4 arms, 5–8 m each, covered with cloth or slats.
3. Tail pole or fantail keeps sails facing the wind.
4. Gearing drives millstone or pump.

### Animal Mill

1. Central post; horizontal beam.
2. Animal (ox, horse) walks in a circle.
3. Beam turns a vertical shaft connected to the millstone.

### Millstone Dressing

1. Cut grooves in a pattern (harps, quarter dress) to shear grain.
2. Sharpen every 100 hours of use.
3. Gap between stones: 0.3–0.6 mm for flour.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Rotating shafts and gears cause entanglement. Guard them.
- Mill dust is explosive — ventilate.
- Millstones can shatter; never over-speed.
- Hearing protection near working mills.

title: Natural Dyes
materialsRequired: Mordant: alum, iron (rusty nails), copper, tannin
Large pot (enamel or stainless — never aluminum for mordanting)
body:
## Overview

Natural dyes color textiles, leather, and paper. Most require a mordant
(metal salt) to fix the color to fiber.

## Prerequisites

- [Rope & Cordage](../survival/rope-cordage.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Plant materials (see table)
- Mordant: alum, iron (rusty nails), copper, tannin
- Large pot (enamel or stainless — never aluminum for mordanting)
- Heat source

## Procedure

### Common Dye Plants

| Color | Source |
|-------|--------|
| Yellow | Onion skin, turmeric, marigold, chamomile |
| Orange | Carrot tops, safflower |
| Red | Madder root, cochineal (insect), beet (poor fastness) |
| Blue | Indigo, woad |
| Green | Overdye yellow with indigo |
| Brown | Walnut hulls, tea, coffee |
| Black | Oak gall + iron mordant |
| Purple | Logwood + iron, elderberry |

### Mordanting

1. Dissolve 10% alum (by fiber weight) in hot water.
2. Soak clean fiber 1 hour at 80°C.
3. Cool; rinse.

### Dyeing

1. Chop plant material; simmer 1 hour.
2. Strain; add wet, mordanted fiber.
3. Simmer 1 hour; stir gently.
4. Cool overnight in the dye bath.
5. Rinse until water runs clear.

### Modifying Color

- Add iron (rusty nails) → darkens, "saddens" colors.
- Add copper → shifts greens.
- Add vinegar → brightens reds.
- Add wood ash → shifts blues.

### Indigo (Vat Dyeing)

1. Ferment indigo with urine or lye + fructose.
2. Dip fiber; it appears yellow-green in the vat.
3. Expose to air; it oxidizes to blue.
4. Repeat dips for deeper blue.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Mordants are metal salts — some (chromium, tin) are toxic.
  Use alum, iron, or copper only.
- Never use aluminum pots for dyeing or mordanting.
- Ventilate when simmering dye plants (some are allergenic).
- Some plants (pokeweed, bloodroot) are toxic; do not handle without gloves.

title: Paper Making
materialsRequired: Fiber: linen rag, cotton, hemp, straw
Mold and deckle (wooden frame with mesh)
body:
## Overview

Paper preserves knowledge. It is made from cellulose fiber (rag, hemp, straw)
beaten into pulp, then pressed and dried.

## Prerequisites

- [Rope & Cordage](../survival/rope-cordage.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Fiber: linen rag, cotton, hemp, straw
- Water
- Wooden beater or mortar
- Mold and deckle (wooden frame with mesh)
- Press
- Sizing (gelatin or starch)

## Procedure

### Preparing Pulp

1. Cut rags into 2 cm squares.
2. Ret in water 24 hours.
3. Beat with a wooden mallet or in a mortar to separate fibers.
4. Dilute in water to 1% consistency.

### Forming Sheets

1. Dip mold into pulp; lift horizontally.
2. Shake side-to-side to interlock fibers.
3. Drain; couch sheet onto felt.
4. Stack sheets between felts.

### Pressing & Drying

1. Press stack to remove water.
2. Hang sheets to dry on a line or board.
3. Dried sheets are brittle; size them.

### Sizing

1. Dip in warm gelatin (3%) or starch solution.
2. Dry. Sized paper resists ink bleed.

### Recycled Paper

1. Tear waste paper; soak 24 hours.
2. Blend in water; strain.
3. Proceed as above; fibers are shorter — mixed sheets may be weaker.

## Safety Notes

- Alkaline pulp can irritate skin — wear gloves for long sessions.
- Mold growth on drying sheets is possible in humid climates; dry thoroughly.
- Do not use treated or painted wood scraps for pulp.

title: Salt Production and Iodization
yield: 20-30 kg of salt per 1,000 L of seawater, depending on salinity and recovery
season: Dry, sunny, windy season for solar evaporation
